newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crude outlook - heading south on weather, Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crude outlook - heading south on weather, Iraq.

text.p: U.S. crudes are likely to head further south this week on above-normal temperature forecasts and final U.N. clearance for Iraqi oil exports, industry sources said Monday.
Bearish news overwhelmed some pockets of bullishness, such as a one-day strike at Royal Dutch/Shell's Berre refinery in southern France, they said.
January West Texas Intermediate was trading around $25.00-10 a barrel Monday morning, down from $25.55-65 late Friday.

"I think we could see prices around $24.20-30 if we take out Friday's lows. There's mild weather in the Northeast and in Europe, and gas oil and heating oil are under pressure," said Warren Tashneck, vice president and manager of Houston-based Fimat Futures USA Inc.
For Dec 12 through 16, the National Weather Service expects above-normal temperatures "over half the lower 48 states," excluding parts of southern California and Pacific Northwest.
The end of a nine-day strike at three French refineries belonging to Elf Aquitaine adds to the bearish scenario, Tashneck said.
The strike put pressure on gasoline prices on both sides of the Atlantic last week, which in turn underpinned U.S. crude prices.
The U.N. go-ahead Monday morning for Iraqi exports is compunding the downturn, even though some market players say they have already discounted the impact of the oft-delayed oil-for-food deal.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali approved the start of Iraqi exports, enabling Baghdad to re-enter the world market for the first time since 1990.
From a fundamental perspective, the U.S. crude outlook is equally bearish.
"We're oriented toward the view that the market balance will weaken," said Ken Miller, senior principal at Houston-based Purvin & Gertz.
"There's more supply coming on than demand," he said, citing anticipated production increases in the North Sea, Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Venezuela.
"The weather and low inventories are carrying us across the winter, but we're headed for a major fall. That's what the balances imply," he said.
He said prices are heading toward $18-20 a barrel range by the second quarter of 1997.
Not everyone is bearish, at least in the near term.
"Unless the funds decide to dump out, the price will have a hard time coming down," said broker John Troland with Houston-based Belmont Crude.
"Don't get in front of the freight train, the train is still moving forward," he said.
